extracted.intended_audience: graduate and advanced undergraduate students and researchers in functional analysis / operator theory
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and exercises concerning compact operators on Banach and Hilbert spaces, Fredholm alternative, spectrum and resolvent, and spectral decomposition of self-adjoint compact operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of compact operator
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounded operator T ∈ L(E, F) is said to be compact if T(BE) has compact closure in F (in the strong topology). The set of all compact operators from E into F is denoted by K(E, F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compactness is tested on the image of the unit ball. Notation: K(E)=K(E,E). This is the central notion used in the chapter; many subsequent results assume this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: K(E,F) is closed linear subspace
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.1: The set K(E, F) is a closed linear subspace of L(E, F) (with the operator norm topology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sum of compact operators is compact; norm-limit of compact operators is compact. Proof sketch: use finite ε-coverings of images of the unit ball and uniform operator-norm convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-rank operator
rubrics_metrics.description: An operator T ∈ L(E, F) is of finite rank if R(T) is finite-dimensional. Every finite-rank operator is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denote finite-rank operators as explicit finite-dimensional images; used to approximate compact operators in some settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of finite-rank operators is compact
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 6.2: If (Tn) is a sequence of finite-rank operators and T ∈ L(E,F) with ||Tn − T||_{L(E,F)} → 0, then T ∈ K(E, F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a sufficient condition for compactness via approximation by finite-rank operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation problem and positive cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The approximation problem: does every compact operator admit norm-approximation by finite-rank operators? Not always (counterexamples exist), but the answer is positive in special cases (e.g., when F is a Hilbert space or F has a Schauder basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When F is a Hilbert space one constructs finite-rank approximations via finite coverings of K=T(BE) and projecting onto the span of covering centers; ||Tε − T|| ≤ 2ε. Citations and classical counterexamples (Enflo) are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-rank approximation of continuous maps with compact image
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a topological space and T: X → F is continuous with T(X) compact in a Banach space F, then for every ε>0 there exists a continuous finite-rank map Tε: X → F with ||Tε(x) − T(x)|| < ε for all x ∈ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via finite ε/2-covering K ⊂ ⋃ B(fi, ε/2) and suitable continuous partition-like weights qi(x) giving Tε(x)=∑ qi(x)fi / ∑ qi(x). Useful for nonlinear analysis (Schauder fixed-point applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition rule for compact operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 6.3: If T ∈ L(E, F) and S ∈ K(F, G) (or T ∈ K(E, F) and S ∈ L(F, G)), then S ◦ T ∈ K(E, G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compactness is preserved when composed with bounded operators on either side; helps build new compact operators from known ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjoint of a compact operator is compact (Schauder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.4 (Schauder): T ∈ K(E, F) iff its adjoint T* ∈ K(F*, E*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Ascoli–Arzelà via the compact set K=T(BE) and equicontinuity of associated function families. Converse also holds by duality; useful for relating properties of T and T*.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact operators map weakly convergent sequences to strongly convergent sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: If un → u weakly in E and T ∈ K(E,F), then T un → T u strongly in F. Conversely, if E is reflexive and T maps weakly convergent sequences to strongly convergent sequences, then T is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterization is often used to verify compactness or to extract strong convergence from weak limits under compact operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riesz lemma (separation from closed subspace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 6.1 (Riesz): If M is a closed linear subspace of a normed vector space E with M ≠ E, then for every ε>0 there exists u with ||u||=1 and dist(u, M) ≥ 1 − ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to construct sequences with no convergent subsequence, and to prove finite-dimensionality results. If M is finite-dimensional or reflexive one can take ε=0; otherwise not necessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact unit ball implies finite-dimensional (Riesz theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.5 (Riesz): If the closed unit ball BE in a normed vector space E is compact, then E is finite-dimensional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Riesz Lemma to build a sequence without convergent subsequence if infinite-dimensional. Fundamental to distinguishing finite vs infinite-dimensional behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fredholm alternative for compact operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.6: For T ∈ K(E): (a) N(I − T) is finite-dimensional; (b) R(I − T) is closed and R(I − T) = N(I − T*)⊥; (c) N(I − T) = {0} ⇔ R(I − T) = E; (d) dim N(I − T) = dim N(I − T*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the dichotomy for solvability of u − T u = f: either unique solution for every f, or homogeneous equation has n independent solutions and inhomogeneous solvable exactly when f is orthogonal to a finite-dimensional subspace. Proof uses compactness to extract convergent subsequences and finite-dimensionality arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Fredholm alternative (solvability conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: The inhomogeneous equation u − T u = f is solvable iff f ∈ N(I − T*)⊥ when N(I − T) has positive finite dimension; if N(I − T) = {0} then u − T u = f has a unique solution for every f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly states orthogonality conditions on the right-hand side as necessary and sufficient solvability criteria in the non-unique homogeneous case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of resolvent, spectrum, eigenvalue
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolvent set ρ(T) = {λ ∈ R: T − λI is bijective}. Spectrum σ(T) = R ho(T). λ is an eigenvalue if N(T − λI) ≠ {0}. The set of eigenvalues is EV(T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic spectral definitions; keep in mind that in infinite-dimensional real spaces EV(T) can be strictly smaller than σ(T); working over C changes some properties (e.g., nonemptiness of spectrum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum bounded and compact
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 6.7: The spectrum σ(T) of a bounded operator T is compact and σ(T) ⊂ [−||T||, ||T||].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses contraction principle: if |λ|>||T|| then T−λI is invertible with bounded inverse. Also ρ(T) is open (stability of invertibility under small perturbations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum of compact operator on infinite-dimensional space
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.8: If T ∈ K(E) and dim E = ∞ then (a) 0 ∈ σ(T); (b) σ(T) \ {0} = EV(T) \ {0} (every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue); (c) either σ(T) = {0}, or σ(T) \ {0} is finite, or σ(T) \ {0} is a sequence converging to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonzero spectrum consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity that can only accumulate at 0. This classifies the possible spectra for compact operators on infinite-dimensional spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonzero spectral points are isolated (lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 6.2: If T ∈ K(E) and (λn) is a sequence of distinct nonzero spectral points with λn → λ then λ = 0. Equivalently, every nonzero point of σ(T) is isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs growing finite-dimensional invariant subspaces spanned by eigenvectors and uses Riesz Lemma to contradict compactness unless limit is 0. Ensures discreteness of nonzero spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-adjoint operator spectral bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and Proposition 6.9: For self-adjoint T ∈ L(H), set m = inf_{|u|=1} (T u, u), M = sup_{|u|=1} (T u, u). Then σ(T) ⊂ [m, M], and m, M ∈ σ(T). Moreover ||T|| = max{|m|, |M|}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Lax–Milgram to show resolvent beyond M (or below m) and a Cauchy–Schwarz type inequality for bilinear form a(u,v) = (Mu − T u, v) to show M ∈ σ(T). This locates the spectrum for self-adjoint operators on the real line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-only spectrum implies zero operator (self-adjoint case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 6.10: If T ∈ L(H) is self-adjoint and σ(T) = {0}, then T = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from Proposition 6.9 since then m = M = 0 so operator norm is zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectral decomposition of compact self-adjoint operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.11: For a separable Hilbert space H and compact self-adjoint T, there exists a Hilbert basis composed of eigenvectors of T. H is the (orthogonal) Hilbert sum of eigenspaces En (including E0 = N(T)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each nonzero eigenspace En is finite-dimensional; the eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal; the span of all eigenspaces is dense. The theorem provides diagonalization and a basis for functional calculus and approximations by finite-rank operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series representation and finite-rank truncations
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: For T compact self-adjoint with eigenvalues (λn) and orthogonal projections un ∈ En, any u ∈ H decomposes u = ∑ un and T u = ∑ λn un. Finite-rank truncations Tk = ∑_{n=1}^k λn P_{En} satisfy ||Tk − T|| ≤ sup_{n≥k+1} |λn| → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an explicit method to approximate T in operator norm by finite-rank operators via spectral truncation; useful for numerical approximation and theoretical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fredholm operator definition and index
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments: A ∈ L(E,F) is Fredholm if N(A) is finite-dimensional and R(A) is closed with finite codimension. The index ind A = dim N(A) − codim R(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: (a) class of Fredholm operators is open in operator norm and index is locally constant; (b) A is invertible modulo finite-rank operators; (c) adding compact perturbations preserves Fredholmness and index; (d) composition of Fredholm operators adds indices. Operators of form I − T with T compact are Fredholm index 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert–Schmidt operator characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments: For separable H, T ∈ L(H) is Hilbert–Schmidt if for a Hilbert basis (en), ∑ |T en|^2 < ∞. The HS norm is basis-independent and every HS operator is compact. On L2(Ω) an integral operator with kernel K∈L2(Ω×Ω) is Hilbert–Schmidt; conversely every HS operator arises from a unique L2 kernel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert–Schmidt class gives a concrete subclass of compact operators with L2-kernel representation, important for examples and applications (Theorem 6.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and ascent of eigenvalues
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments: For T ∈ K(E) and λ ≠ 0, the chain of nullspaces N((T − λI)^k) increases up to a finite p (the ascent) and then stabilizes. Geometric multiplicity = dim N(T − λI), algebraic multiplicity = dim N((T − λI)^p); for self-adjoint T on Hilbert spaces these multiplicities coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies notions of multiplicity for eigenvalues of compact operators; in the self-adjoint case there are no Jordan blocks and algebraic/geometric multiplicities agree.
